title: Design patterns and SOLID (language-independent)
seriesDescription: Language-independent interview topics (concepts, SQL, design, AI engineering): no Java and no Python code or library names.
description: Pattern intents, creational patterns, Strategy, Observer, Command with undo/redo, Proxy vs Adapter vs Decorator, dependency injection and the SOLID principles, with the classic traps.
source: Gang of Four; Robert C. Martin: SOLID; Refactoring.Guru; Head First Design Patterns; GeeksforGeeks design pattern interview list

questions.prompt: Match each design pattern with its intent.

right.text: Exactly one instance with a global access point
Defer to a method or subclass to decide which concrete class to create
Construct a complex object step by step, often with many optional parts
Interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, chosen at runtime
One-to-many notification when a subject changes state
Wrap a request as an object so it can be queued, logged or undone
Convert the interface of one class into another that clients expect

questions.explanation: Each pattern has a recognisable everyday example: a runtime object (singleton), a static creation helper (factory), a string builder (builder), a comparator (strategy), event listeners (observer) and an undo stack (command).

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: The Strategy pattern lets a program swap algorithms at runtime without long if/else chains.
questions.reason: The context object holds a reference to a strategy interface and delegates the work to it.

whys.a: Correct: delegation to an interface-typed field is the mechanism that makes swapping possible.
whys.b: R is the explanation of A, not an unrelated fact.

questions.explanation: Typical interview example: payment methods or pricing rules. In most languages a function or lambda can play the strategy.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Abstract Factory is the right pattern when a program must create families of related objects that are meant to be used together, such as widgets for one UI theme.
questions.reason: Factory Method defers the choice of the concrete class to a subclass.

whys.a: Not chosen: R is true but it describes a different pattern, so it does not explain A.
whys.b: Correct: both statements are true, but R describes Factory Method, which is a related yet separate pattern (Abstract Factory is often built from several factory methods).
whys.c: Not chosen: R is a true statement about Factory Method.
whys.d: Not chosen: A is true, because creating consistent product families is the stated intent of Abstract Factory.

questions.explanation: Remember: Factory Method = one product, subclass decides; Abstract Factory = a family of products from one factory object; Builder = step-by-step construction.

questions.prompt: A class implements the same interface as a heavy ImageLoader, creates the real loader only on first use and checks the caller permissions before delegating. Which pattern is this?

options.why: Correct: same interface, controls access to the real subject (lazy creation plus protection).
Wrong: an adapter converts one interface into a different one the client expects; here the interface stays the same.
Wrong: a facade offers a new simplified interface to a whole subsystem, not a stand-in for one object.
Wrong: composite lets clients treat a tree of parts and wholes uniformly, which is unrelated to lazy access control.

questions.explanation: A decorator adds behaviour that the client chose, while a proxy controls access and decides when the real object is created. Lazy loading and access-control layers are typical proxies.

questions.text: Instead of creating collaborators with {1} inside a class, pass them in through the constructor (constructor {2}); tests then supply a {3} or fake.
questions.explanation: Manual DI is just wiring objects in a main function or a composition root. Container frameworks automate the lookup, but the principle (depend on abstractions, receive them from outside) is the same.

questions.prompt: Match each SOLID principle with its meaning.

right.text: A class should have one reason to change
Add behaviour by extension, not by editing tested code
Subtypes must be usable wherever the base type is expected without breaking callers
Prefer several small client-specific interfaces over one fat interface
High-level modules depend on abstractions, not on concrete low-level classes
Every class must be declared final

questions.explanation: A rectangle/square subclass that breaks setWidth is the usual Liskov example; constructor injection is the usual way to apply Dependency Inversion.

questions.prompt: An editor keeps an undo stack and a redo stack. The user executes commands A, B, C, D, E, then does undo, undo, redo, and finally executes a new command F. How many commands are on the undo stack at the end?
questions.explanation: After A-E: undo has 5. Two undos move E and D to redo (undo = A,B,C). Redo moves D back (undo = A,B,C,D, redo = E). Executing F pushes it and clears the redo stack: undo = A,B,C,D,F = 5 and redo = 0.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: An Observer implementation that holds strong references to its listeners can cause a memory leak.
questions.reason: Listeners are garbage collected automatically as soon as they leave their local scope, even while they are still registered.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (the lapsed listener problem); R is false, because a registered listener is still reachable from the subject.

questions.explanation: Always provide an unsubscribe operation, or hold listeners through weak references so the subject does not keep them alive.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: The Dependency Inversion Principle says high-level modules should create their low-level dependencies directly.
questions.reason: Both high-level and low-level modules should depend on abstractions rather than on each other's details.

whys.a: This option says both statements are true and R explains A, which does not match: A is false: inversion means depending on abstractions that are supplied from outside; R is the correct statement of the principle.
whys.b: This option says both statements are true but R does not explain A, which does not match: A is false: inversion means depending on abstractions that are supplied from outside; R is the correct statement of the principle.
whys.c: This option says A is true and R is false, which does not match: A is false: inversion means depending on abstractions that are supplied from outside; R is the correct statement of the principle.
whys.d: Correct: A is false: inversion means depending on abstractions that are supplied from outside; R is the correct statement of the principle.

questions.explanation: Inject an interface (constructor injection) so the high-level policy does not know the concrete detail.

questions.prompt: A legacy component exposes fetchAll(), but your code is written against a Repository interface that declares list(). You want to reuse the legacy component without changing it. Which pattern fits?

options.why: Correct: an adapter converts one interface into the one the client expects.
A facade simplifies a large subsystem behind a smaller interface; it does not translate one interface into another.
Singleton restricts instances and says nothing about interface conversion.
Observer notifies subscribers of changes; it does not reconcile mismatched interfaces.

questions.explanation: Adapter changes the interface, Decorator keeps it and adds behaviour, Proxy keeps it and controls access.

options.why: It controls how and how many instances are created.
It decides which concrete class to instantiate.
It constructs a complex object step by step.
It is behavioural: it notifies dependents of state changes.
It is structural: it converts one interface into another.

questions.explanation: Creational patterns deal with object creation, structural ones with composition, behavioural ones with interaction.

questions.prompt: Decorator and Proxy often have the same structure, wrapping an object behind the same interface, and differ mainly in intent.

options.why: Correct: a decorator adds behaviour, a proxy controls access, yet both implement the wrapped type's interface.
Their class diagrams are almost identical; the intent is what distinguishes them.

questions.explanation: Name the intent in an interview: add behaviour (Decorator) versus guard, defer or remote access (Proxy).

questions.prompt: A subject keeps its observers in a plain list with no duplicate check. Observer A subscribes twice, B subscribes once and C subscribes once. Then B unsubscribes (removing one entry) and the subject publishes 2 events. How many notification calls are made in total?
questions.explanation: After the changes the list holds A, A, C, which is 3 calls per event, so 2 events make 6 calls.

questions.prompt: Write pseudocode for undo() in an editor that keeps a stack named history of executed commands and a stack named redo: it must reverse the most recent command and make it available for redo.

checks.label: pops the last command from history
pushes it onto the redo stack

questions.model:
undo():
  if history is empty: return
  cmd = history.pop()
  cmd.undo()
  redo.push(cmd)
questions.explanation: Redo does the reverse: pop from redo, execute, push to history. Executing a brand-new command clears the redo stack.
